one_liner: Type-safe C++ formatting library (positional fmt and concatenating write) that beats IOStreams and Boost.Format; mixed against printf.
what_it_does: FastFormat formats arguments into any sink (std::string, char buffers, std::ostream and others) through two APIs: fastformat::fmt(sink, "{0} {1}", a, b) with numbered, reusable placeholders, and fastformat::write(sink, a, ", ", b) which simply concatenates. Arguments are converted through STLSoft 'shims', so any type with a string-access or filter_type shim works without format specifiers. It is a different interface from printf and IOStreams, not a drop-in.
how_it_is_fast: Each argument is turned into a (pointer, length) string slice without a format-specifier interpreter; the sink then sums the slice lengths, reserves once and appends (shims/action/fmt_slices/generic_string.hpp), so a std::string target is grown a single time. Format patterns are parsed once and cached in a process-wide std::map (src/fmt_cache.cpp), so repeated literal patterns skip parsing, unlike Boost.Format which re-parses per call. Integers go through STLSoft's integer_to_string; doubles and pointers are not converted natively but by calling sprintf("%G") and snprintf("%p").
when_to_use: Building strings from many string-like pieces (std::string, C strings, string views, long payloads) where knowing lengths up front and one reservation beat sprintf's strlen-and-copy plus a second copy into std::string (the 6.9x scenario was ten strings including a 1000-char one)
Replacing Boost.Format or IOStreams string building in hot paths with a type-safe API (5-17x and roughly 2-10x on the author's tables)
Code already built on STLSoft or Pantheios, where the shim mechanism lets your own types format without extra glue
I18N-style positional patterns where an argument is referenced several times ({0} reused)
when_not_to_use: Floating-point or pointer formatting: FastFormat calls sprintf("%G") / snprintf("%p") internally, so it cannot beat printf there and lost to it on average in exactly those scenarios (2 and 4)
New projects that can use {fmt} or C++20 std::format: same positional, type-safe model, maintained, with native fast float formatting

Builds on Windows with the current repo: the CMake build stops with 'Use of CMake on Windows not currently supported' and the legacy makefiles were removed, although most of the published wins over printf came from Visual C++ rows
Projects that cannot take STLSoft (and xTests for the tests) as dependencies or that need a packaged, released library (latest is 0.7.4 RC 6 from February 2024)
Formatting char or bool values without writing your own shim: those conversion shims are marked 'Feature not yet implemented' in fastformat.hpp

integration.form: static lib (src/*.cpp: api, fmt_cache, memory_pool, replacements, snprintf) plus headers
integration.dependencies: STLSoft headers (1.9.121+ per INSTALL.md; CMake looks for STLSoft 0.10.8+ and xTests 0.21.2+ when BUILD_TESTING is on); Boost and Loki only for the comparison benchmarks
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 11), CMake 3.20; library built with -Werror -Wall -Wextra -pedantic on GCC/Clang
integration.platforms: Unix-like (Linux, macOS) via CMake; Windows only historically (CMake build refuses Windows)
integration.thread_safety: The pattern cache is a process-wide std::map guarded by a platformstl thread_mutex only when FASTFORMAT_MT is defined (Unix: UNIXSTL_USING_PTHREADS; Windows: _MT/_REENTRANT/__MT__); without it a null_mutex is used and concurrent fmt() calls are unsafe. Sinks are not synchronised (ostream sink locking is on the TODO list).

gotchas: Benchmark harness: the scenarios FastFormat loses against the printf family (2: float height, 4: pointer) are the ones where FastFormat itself delegates to sprintf("%G") and snprintf("%p"), so those losses are structural, not noise; the 'Streams (snprintf())' column actually times unbounded ::sprintf into a fixed stack buffer plus a std::string copy, and output equality is checked only in debug builds (#ifndef NDEBUG).

Benchmark harness: the IOStreams column constructs a fresh std::stringstream per call and the Format column always hits its pattern cache with one literal pattern, which flatters the IOStreams and Boost.Format ratios relative to code that reuses a stream or has many distinct patterns.
Doubles print with %G, not %g: 6 significant digits, uppercase exponent and INF/NAN, so output differs from printf("%g") and is not round-trip safe.
Every fmt() call takes the pattern-cache mutex in MT builds and the cache grows without bound with each distinct pattern string; use write() or literal patterns in hot or multi-threaded code.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: {fmt} is the catalogued sibling with the same type-safe, positional API and is far faster on doubles (20x over sprintf per its benchmark, where FastFormat just calls sprintf); pick FastFormat only for string-concatenation-heavy code already on STLSoft/Pantheios, and use Ryu, Dragonbox or the to_chars libraries for number conversion.
verified_claims_summary: The author's 2008-2009 page (FastFormat 0.2.1 beta 6; GCC 4.1/4.2 on Ubuntu x86/x64 and Visual C++ 6/9 on Windows x86/x64; no CPU or flags) times seven std::string-building scenarios at 100,000 iterations each: averaged over the five rows FastFormat.Format is 5-17x faster than Boost.Format, about 2-10x faster than IOStreams, and 0.66-6.87x versus the printf family, losing on the float and pointer scenarios and, per the record's derivation, losing to glibc sprintf in 11 of 14 GCC cells.
status_note: BSD-3-Clause and still buildable on Unix with CMake (added February 2024), but effectively dormant since 2017 apart from boilerplate commits (last 2026-08-04), never released past 0.7.4 RC 6, and its speed evidence is from 15-year-old compilers.
